doc_name: Murders of Yuna and Minu Jo
text: In August 2022, the bodies of two children, Minu and Yuna Jo, were discovered in suitcases at a storage unit auction in Auckland, New Zealand, where the suitcases were purchased by a family from Safe Store Papatoetoe. The children, born in March 2012 and September 2009 respectively, were last seen by relatives on 26 April 2018, and their last recorded activity in Minecraft was on 27 June 2018. Hakyung Lee, the mother of the children, was born as Ji Eun Lee and migrated to New Zealand in 1993 at age 13, returning to South Korea in 1998 for university and later returning to New Zealand to study hospitality, where she met her future husband Ian Jo at a church and became a Sunday school teacher. They married in 2006 and lived in West Auckland, settling in Papatoetoe after the birth of their children. Minu had a speech impediment due to cleft palate. Ian Jo died from cancer in November 2017, and Lee did not inform her children of his death, becoming suicidal, isolated, and allegedly insane, believing it was best for her children to die with him. In December 2017, Lee took her children on a two-month holiday in South Korea, spending NZ$32,000, and later visited Taupō, the Gold Coast, and Queenstown in June 2018. The children were last seen on 26 April 2018. Lee killed them around late June 2018 by serving them juice mixed with the antidepressant Nortriptyline, and wrapped their bodies in suitcases, hiding them in a storage unit. The pathologist could not determine whether the children died from the drug or were killed by other means after being incapacitated. Both prosecution and defence agree Lee caused the deaths, but disagree on whether she was insane at the time. After the killings, Lee attempted suicide, changed her name to Hakyung Lee, and returned to South Korea in July 2018 on a business class flight, spending money on beauty treatments and being diagnosed with depression. In 2021, she began a relationship via a dating app, which she described as traumatic and involving assault. In mid-June 2022, Lee’s mother learned from her pastor that Lee was in a South Korean psychiatric ward and visited her, during which Lee asked for contact lenses, clothes, and a phone. After returning to New Zealand, Lee’s mother was contacted by police about the discovery of the children’s remains. On 11 August 2022, the bodies were found in Moncrieff Ave, Clendon Park, and the family who bought the suitcases was not connected to the deaths. Police estimated the children may have been dead for up to four years. In September 2023, interim name suppression for the children was lifted by Coroner Tania Tetitaha, revealing their names as Minu Jo and Yuna Jo, aged about six and eight at the time of death. On 22 August 2022, New Zealand Police confirmed Lee had returned to South Korea in 2018. On 15 September 2022, Lee was arrested in Ulsan, South Korea, on suspicion of "crimes against humanity" and faced two murder charges in New Zealand. South Korean Minister of Justice Han Dong-hoon approved her extradition in November 2022, following Seoul High Court approval after she granted written consent. On 29 November 2022, Lee was extradited to New Zealand, with "significant pieces of evidence" submitted to New Zealand authorities. On 30 November 2022, she appeared in Manukau District Court, entered no plea, and was remanded into custody with identities of the suspect, her children, and an unidentified relative suppressed. On 14 December, she pleaded not guilty and remained in custody. On 3 May 2023, she stated she would prove her innocence, and on 8 May, her lawyers requested continued name suppression, which was denied by the Court of Appeal on 19 July 2023. On 25 September 2023, Coroner Tania Tetitaha lifted interim name suppression for the children, prompting two New Zealand relatives to apply for name suppression. Lee’s trial was initially scheduled for 29 April 2024 but was postponed to 8 September 2025. On 8 September 2025, she pleaded not guilty at the Auckland High Court, with Justice Geoffrey Venning indicating she would raise an insanity defence. She represented herself with court-appointed lawyers Lorraine Smith and Chris Wilkinson-Smith, while the Crown was represented by solicitor Natalie Walker and prosecutors Jay Tausi and Jong Kim. The Crown opened with evidence that toxicology tests showed the children died from homicide linked to Nortriptyline, noting Lee had been prescribed 60 tablets in August 2017 due to sleep difficulties. The Crown argued Lee knew her actions were wrong, citing her behaviour including hiring a storage unit, hiding the bodies, changing her name, and returning to South Korea on a business class flight. The defence, led by stand-by counsel Lorraine Smith, argued Lee was insane due to mental deterioration after her husband’s death, believing it was best for her children to die to avoid an unhappy, parentless future. The defence cited Lee’s previous suicide attempts, including one after her father’s death, and her belief that she caused her father and husband’s deaths and her son’s cleft palate, indicating a disconnection from reality. The Crown called witnesses including Safe Store staff Shi-Hui Cong, teacher Mary Robertson, Lee’s brother-in-law Jimmy Sae Wook Cho, his wife Bo Ram Lim, friend Gina Min, forensic toxicologist Helen Poulsen, family doctor Rama Velalagan, nurses Lin Ni, Kayleen Palatchie, and Natalie Woodward, and others including Lee’s mother Choon Ja Lee, forensic accountant Andrew Yoon, South Korean Detective Sergeant Sung Kyu Hwang, Detective Sergeant Ryan Singleton, and digital forensic analyst Damian Govender. The defence’s sole witness, psychiatrist Dr. Yvette Kelly, argued Lee met the criteria for insanity under Section 23 of the Crimes Act 1961, stating she confessed to killing the children with Nortriptyline-infused juice but was legally insane at the time. The Crown rebutted with forensic psychiatrist Erik Monasterio, who testified Lee did not display symptoms of schizophrenia. On 22 September, closing arguments were delivered, with Walker asserting Lee was not insane, citing her actions and lies to family and doctors, and Monasterio’s testimony that Lee lacked psychosis or awareness of moral wrongfulness. Smith argued Lee’s mental state deteriorated over seven months after her husband’s death, leading her to believe killing her children was the only solution. The jury began deliberating on 23 September and, after three and a half hours, convicted Lee of murdering Minu and Yuna Jo. Justice Venning confirmed the verdict and remanded her into custody until sentencing on 26 November 2025. She was sentenced to life imprisonment and will be eligible for parole after 17 years.
